question:
Microsoft Hiring Manager plus Bar Raiser onsite round for a Senior SWE role (L65). Alongside a **website activity analytics system design** (18-month lookback, 5-minute granularity, filters by language and country), the interviewer asked about **transformer architecture basics**, the **effect of temperature, top-k and top-p on LLM outputs**, and how to **measure AI tool adoption and the impact of agentic AI**.

This write-up covers the AI/ML part: explain the sampling controls and propose a measurement approach.
lookingFor: Working knowledge of how LLMs generate text, not only API parameter names.
Ability to reason about trade-offs: determinism versus diversity.
Product-minded metrics thinking: adoption, quality, impact, cost.
Awareness of confounders and vanity metrics.
Clear communication of technical ideas to a manager audience.
answer:
**Transformer basics.** Text is tokenised and embedded; positional information is added. Each layer has multi-head self-attention, `softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) V`, which lets every token weigh every other token, followed by a feed-forward network, with residual connections and layer normalisation. Decoder-only LLMs use causal masking and predict the next-token distribution.

**Sampling controls.** The model outputs logits; a softmax turns them into probabilities, and a token is sampled.
- **Temperature** divides logits before softmax. Below 1 sharpens the distribution (more deterministic, near-greedy as it approaches 0); above 1 flattens it (more diverse, more risk of incoherence).
- **Top-k** keeps only the k most probable tokens, renormalises, then samples. Fixed k can be too loose when the model is confident and too tight when many tokens are plausible.
- **Top-p (nucleus)** keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability is at least p, so the candidate set adapts to confidence.
Typically used together: low temperature for code and extraction, higher for brainstorming. Many providers advise tuning temperature or top-p, not both.

**Measuring AI tool adoption.** Define the eligible population, then track:
- *Reach:* weekly active users over eligible users, new versus retained.
- *Depth:* sessions per user, features used, suggestion acceptance rate.
- *Outcomes:* cycle time, PR throughput, time to resolve tickets, defect and rollback rate, measured against a baseline or control group (staggered rollout or A/B).
- *Quality and cost:* review effort, incidents, spend per active user, satisfaction surveys.

**Agentic AI impact.** Task completion rate, human-intervention or escalation rate, correctness on sampled audits, time saved per task, cost per completed task, and failure modes.

Warn against vanity metrics (raw usage, lines generated) and confounders such as novelty effects and self-selection.
followUps: Why does temperature 0 not always give identical outputs?
When would you prefer top-p over top-k?
How would you run an A/B test for a coding assistant rollout?
How do you detect that an agent is quietly producing wrong results?
What is the KV cache and why does it matter for latency?
